title: Money and markets
description: Start with shares, prices and the way a trade happens.
introduction:
[Course home](README.md) · Previous: course introduction · [Next: option contracts](beginner/02_CONTRACTS.md)

Start here with a pen, paper, and an ordinary calculator. Read **one lesson per session**, taking 5–10 minutes to read, work the example, answer, and explain the idea aloud. You may stop after one lesson. ABC and every price below are fictional. No brokerage account, coding, or real money is needed. Stock examples ignore dividends, fees, and taxes unless stated.

lessons.title: your first goal is understanding
lessons.body:
**Time: 5–10 minutes. One idea:** learning a trading skill and making money are different outcomes.

An investment can lose value. For now your job is to understand a decision before making it. Completing this course cannot promise a profit. Your first measurable goal is: “I can explain an example and solve a changed version.” Keep any money needed for everyday life outside these exercises. The [SEC explains investment risk](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/what-risk).

**Worked example:** Mira uses $100 of imaginary money in a notebook. Her first answer is wrong; she fixes it and solves a new example. She has learned something. Her actual bank balance has changed by $0.

**Try it:** Dev doubles an imaginary $50 by guessing. Can that one result establish that Dev understands trading? Explain in one sentence.

<details>
<summary>Answer — open after your attempt</summary>

No. Imaginary $50 becoming $100 records one outcome; it does not show an understood or repeatable decision process. Ask Dev to explain the risk and solve an unfamiliar example.

</details>

lessons.title: a share is a piece of ownership
lessons.body:
**Time: 5–10 minutes. One idea:** a stock share represents ownership in a company.

A company is a business. A **share** is one unit of its stock. The share's market price can rise or fall; ownership is not a promise that you will get your purchase money back. Our imaginary business is called ABC. [SEC: stocks](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/investment-products/stocks).

**Worked example:** Imagine ABC has exactly 100 equal shares and you own 2. Your slice is `2 ÷ 100 = 0.02`, or 2% of those shares. This tiny made-up company makes the idea visible; real public companies often have far more shares.

**Try it:** A fictional business has 200 equal shares. You own 10. What percentage of those shares do you own?

<details>
<summary>Answer — open after your attempt</summary>

`10 ÷ 200 = 0.05 = 5%`. You own 5% of the shares in this simplified example. This does not tell you what their future price will be.

</details>

lessons.title: turn a share price into total dollars
lessons.body:
**Time: 5–10 minutes. One idea:** price per share and total position value are different quantities.

Multiply the number of shares by the dollars for each share. Write the units: `shares × dollars per share = dollars`. A **position** just means an amount of an investment you hold. This lesson uses arithmetic, not a forecast.

**Worked example:** You buy 3 ABC shares for $20 each. Cost is `3 × $20 = $60`. If each is later worth $18, the position is worth `3 × $18 = $54`. The change is `$54 − $60 = −$6`, a $6 loss before costs.

**Try it:** You buy 4 shares at $15 each. They later reach $17 each. Find the starting cost, new value, and dollar gain before costs.

<details>
<summary>Answer — open after your attempt</summary>

Starting cost: `4 × $15 = $60`. New value: `4 × $17 = $68`. Gain: `$68 − $60 = $8`. The quoted price rose by $2 per share, so four shares gained $8.

</details>

lessons.title: a percentage needs a starting amount
lessons.body:
**Time: 5–10 minutes. One idea:** percentage return compares a gain or loss with what you started with.

Use `return = (ending value − starting value) ÷ starting value × 100%`. Here, “return” means the percentage change in value, ignoring costs and other cash flows. The denominator—the number below the division sign—is the starting value.

**Worked example:** $80 becomes $88. Gain is `$88 − $80 = $8`. Return is `$8 ÷ $80 = 0.10 = 10%`. If $80 instead becomes $72, return is `−$8 ÷ $80 = −10%`.

**Try it:** A hypothetical position falls from $50 to $40. What percentage did it lose? What percentage rise from $40 would restore $50?

<details>
<summary>Answer — open after your attempt</summary>

Loss: `($40 − $50) ÷ $50 = −20%`. Recovery: `($50 − $40) ÷ $40 = 25%`. The dollar change is $10 both ways, but the starting amount changes. A 20% fall and 20% rise do not cancel.

</details>

lessons.title: an ETF share and an index are different things
lessons.body:
**Time: 5–10 minutes. One idea:** a fund can have shares you buy, while an index is a calculated measure.

An **exchange-traded fund (ETF)** pools investments and has shares that trade on an exchange. An **index** measures a chosen group using a calculation. An ETF may aim to track an index, but the index itself is not a share. [SEC: ETF](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/glossary/exchange-traded-fund-etf), [SEC: market index](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/glossary/market-index).

**Worked example:** Our fictional ABC Index displays 1,000 points. A separate fictional fund, ABC Basket ETF, trades at $25 per share. Buying 2 ETF shares costs `2 × $25 = $50` before fees. You bought fund shares; you did not buy two units of the index's 1,000-point reading.

**Try it:** A fictional index reads 2,500 points, while a fund following it trades at $40 a share. What does buying 3 fund shares cost before fees, and what do you own?

<details>
<summary>Answer — open after your attempt</summary>

`3 × $40 = $120`. You own three shares of the fund. You do not own three shares of the calculated index, and the index level is not the ETF's share price.

</details>

lessons.title: your broker connects your order to markets
lessons.body:
**Time: 5–10 minutes. One idea:** your account provider and a trading venue have different jobs.

A **broker** handles your customer account and orders. An **exchange** is a trading venue with rules for matching trading interest. Seeing a button in a broker's app does not mean a trade has happened; an order must actually receive a **fill**, meaning an execution. [SEC: market participants](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/how-stock-markets-work/market-participants).

**Worked example:** Leena enters a practice instruction to buy 1 ABC share. Her notebook shows “submitted” and zero shares. Then the simulated order fills at $30. Only after that fill does her notebook show 1 share and a $30 purchase, before fees.

**Try it:** A practice broker screen shows an order to buy 2 shares as “open, unfilled.” How many shares did that order buy so far?

<details>
<summary>Answer — open after your attempt</summary>

Zero. An unfilled instruction is not a completed purchase. The requested quantity is 2; the executed quantity is 0.

</details>

lessons.title: buying and selling have different displayed prices
lessons.body:
**Time: 5–10 minutes. One idea:** the bid–ask spread creates a trading cost.

The **bid** is a displayed buying price from the market; the **ask** is a displayed selling price. You might buy at the ask and sell at the bid. Their difference is the **spread**. Displayed prices and available quantities can change before an order fills. [SEC: bid and ask](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/glossary/ask-price).

**Worked example:** One ABC share is quoted $19 bid / $20 ask. Buy one at $20, then immediately sell at the unchanged $19 bid. Result: `$19 − $20 = −$1` before fees. The business did not need to change for that loss to happen.

**Try it:** A share shows $29.50 bid / $30 ask. What is the loss from buying 2 at the ask and immediately selling 2 at the unchanged bid, before fees?

<details>
<summary>Answer — open after your attempt</summary>

Buy cost: `2 × $30 = $60`. Sale proceeds: `2 × $29.50 = $59`. Loss: `$59 − $60 = −$1`, or $0.50 for each share. This assumes both displayed prices have enough size and remain available.

</details>

lessons.title: a limit controls price, not whether you trade
lessons.body:
**Time: 5–10 minutes. One idea:** a limit order states your worst acceptable execution price.

A buy limit sets the highest price you permit; a sell limit sets the lowest. The order may never fill. A **market order** asks for prompt execution at available prices without the same price limit. [SEC: types of orders](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/how-stock-markets-work/types-orders).

**Worked example:** ABC's ask is $10. You write a practice buy limit of $9.80 for one share. If a seller accepts $9.80, it can fill there. If no one sells at $9.80 or lower while your order is active, you buy nothing. Your limit does not turn the ask into $9.80.

**Try it:** Your practice sell limit is $12 per share. Can a normal fill occur at $12.20? At $11.90? Is any fill guaranteed?

<details>
<summary>Answer — open after your attempt</summary>

$12.20 is permitted because it is above your $12 minimum. $11.90 is below that minimum and is not permitted by the limit. A fill is not guaranteed.

</details>

checkpoint:
## Checkpoint 1: try five new questions

Close the lessons and show your reasoning. All numerical examples ignore fees and dividends.

1. You buy 5 ABC shares for $12 each. Their price reaches $13. Find cost, new value, dollar gain, and percentage return.
2. Does a reading of 3,000 on an index mean you own a share worth $3,000? Explain.
3. A practice share quote is $7.80 bid / $8 ask. Find the unchanged ask-to-bid loss for 3 shares.
4. **Safety:** A buy limit is $7.90 while the ask is $8. Are you guaranteed to own shares at $7.90? What maximum price does the limit authorize before fees?
5. **Safety:** An order is submitted but unfilled. Did you buy anything, and does passing this checkpoint establish that you can make money trading?

<details>
<summary>Checkpoint 1 worked key — open after all five attempts</summary>

1. Cost `5 × $12 = $60`; value `5 × $13 = $65`; gain `$5`; return `$5 ÷ $60 × 100% = 8⅓%`.
2. No. The index is a calculated reference level. Owning fund or company shares is a different thing.
3. Cost `3 × $8 = $24`; proceeds `3 × $7.80 = $23.40`; loss `$0.60`.
4. No fill is guaranteed. If the buy limit fills, the purchase price is at most $7.90 per share, excluding fees.
5. No shares were bought by that unfilled order. Passing demonstrates these concepts, not profitable trading.

</details>

**Pass rule:** answer all five correctly and explain both safety items without notes. For an error, reread only that lesson, explain the missed step, and ask your tutor for a changed-number version. Save the new attempt before checking it; repeat until every item is correct. Move on at your pace.

title: Meet the option contract
description: Learn calls, puts and the details of one contract.
introduction:
[Previous: money and markets](beginner/01_MARKETS.md) · [Course home](README.md) · [Next: value and profit](beginner/03_PROFIT.md)

Take one 5–10 minute lesson at a time. These lessons use fictional ABC **standard U.S. stock options with a 100-share deliverable and premium multiplier 100**, unless a question says information is missing. All examples ignore fees and taxes. Learn the meaning before doing more arithmetic. No orders are part of this section.

lessons.title: an option is a contract tied to something else
lessons.body:
**Time: 5–10 minutes. One idea:** the option and its underlying are separate things.

The **underlying** is the asset or measure an option refers to. An ABC stock option refers to ABC shares. Owning that option is not the same as owning ABC stock. The option gives a right defined by its contract; later lessons explain that right. [OIC: what is an option?](https://www.optionseducation.org/optionsoverview/what-is-an-option).

**Worked example:** A shop offers you a written right to buy a bicycle next month for a stated price. Holding the paper is different from owning the bicycle. Similarly, an ABC stock option is a contract about ABC shares; it is not already 100 shares sitting in your account. This is an analogy, not a tradable bicycle option.

**Try it:** Nia owns one ABC call option and has not bought any shares or used the option's right. Does this alone mean Nia owns 100 ABC shares?

<details>
<summary>Answer — open after your attempt</summary>

No. Nia owns one option contract. The underlying is ABC stock, but a contract tied to stock and ownership of the stock are different positions.

</details>

lessons.title: a call gives its buyer a right to buy
lessons.body:
**Time: 5–10 minutes. One idea:** a stock call buyer has a purchase right.

A **call** gives its buyer the right to buy the specified shares at the contract's agreed price, under its terms. That agreed price is the **strike price**. Using the right is called **exercise**. The buyer pays for the right; the option does not promise a profit. [OIC: long call](https://www.optionseducation.org/strategies/all-strategies/long-call).

**Worked example:** One standard ABC $40 call gives its holder the right to buy 100 shares at $40 each. If exercised, the strike payment is `100 × $40 = $4,000` for 100 shares. This payment is separate from what the call itself costs.

**Try it:** What purchase right does one standard ABC $35 call give its buyer? State shares, price per share, and total strike payment if exercised.

<details>
<summary>Answer — open after your attempt</summary>

The right to buy 100 ABC shares at $35 each under the contract terms. Exercise requires `100 × $35 = $3,500` strike cash. That is not the option's purchase premium.

</details>

lessons.title: a put gives its buyer a right to sell
lessons.body:
**Time: 5–10 minutes. One idea:** a stock put buyer has a sale right.

A **put** gives its buyer the right to sell the specified shares at the strike, under the contract terms. Call means a right to buy; put means a right to sell. You can buy either kind of option. [OIC: long put](https://www.optionseducation.org/strategies/all-strategies/long-put).

**Worked example:** One standard ABC $30 put gives its holder the right to sell 100 shares for $30 each. If a holder with 100 shares exercises, those shares leave and `100 × $30 = $3,000` strike cash arrives. We will study what happens without owned shares in [operations](beginner/05_OPERATIONS.md).

**Try it:** A learner owns 100 ABC shares and one standard $25 put. If the put is exercised, what share and strike-cash movements occur, ignoring the premium?

<details>
<summary>Answer — open after your attempt</summary>

The holder delivers 100 ABC shares and receives `100 × $25 = $2,500`. A put is a right to sell shares, even though the holder initially bought the option.

</details>

lessons.title: the strike is a contract term
lessons.body:
**Time: 5–10 minutes. One idea:** distinguish the strike from the changing stock price.

The **strike** is the price specified for exercise. The **stock price** is the current market price of the underlying. They are different fields. The stock moving does not, by itself, reset your contract's strike. Corporate actions can require contract adjustments; defer those to [operations](beginner/05_OPERATIONS.md). [OIC: options basics](https://www.optionseducation.org/optionsoverview/options-basics).

**Worked example:** ABC trades at $48 and a call has strike $50. Tomorrow ABC trades at $53. For the same unadjusted contract, its strike remains $50. The stock moved by `$53 − $48 = $5`; the agreed exercise price did not move by $5.

**Try it:** ABC moves from $60 to $56. An existing unadjusted put has a $58 strike. What is its strike after this ordinary market move?

<details>
<summary>Answer — open after your attempt</summary>

$58. The market price is now $56; the contract still specifies $58. Keep these in separate notebook columns.

</details>

lessons.title: the right has an expiration
lessons.body:
**Time: 5–10 minutes. One idea:** an option does not last indefinitely.

The **expiration** is when the contract ends under its rules. Two options on ABC with the same strike can have different expirations. An expired option does not wait for your prediction to become right. Exact last trading times and exercise cutoffs belong on the operations checklist; the date alone is not the full procedure. [OIC: what is an option?](https://www.optionseducation.org/optionsoverview/what-is-an-option).

**Worked example:** In a made-up calendar, one $50 ABC call expires Friday A and another expires Friday B, a week later. ABC rises the Monday after Friday A. That later rise cannot bring the expired Friday A contract back to life.

**Try it:** You predict a rise within two months but study an option that expires after one week. If the stock rises only in the second month, does that revive the expired option?

<details>
<summary>Answer — open after your attempt</summary>

No. A correct eventual direction does not extend an expired contract. The timing of the move matters because the option has an ending date.

</details>

lessons.title: the premium quote is not the contract's dollar cost
lessons.body:
**Time: 5–10 minutes. One idea:** use the premium multiplier to convert a quote into dollars.

The **premium** is the option's price. For our standard contracts it is quoted per share, with a multiplier of 100. One contract's premium dollars equal `quoted premium × multiplier`. Check the actual multiplier for a real contract; the number 100 is an assumption in these examples. [SEC: stock-options introduction](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins-63).

**Worked example:** One call is bought for $1.20 quoted premium. With multiplier 100, payment is `$1.20 × 100 = $120`, before fees. That $120 buys the option right. It does not pay the separate strike cash required if shares are purchased through exercise.

**Try it:** A standard put has a $0.85 premium quote and multiplier 100. What do two contracts cost before fees?

<details>
<summary>Answer — open after your attempt</summary>

One costs `$0.85 × 100 = $85`; two cost `2 × $85 = $170`. A quote below $1 can still represent tens of dollars per contract.

</details>

lessons.title: identify the exact contract
lessons.body:
**Time: 5–10 minutes. One idea:** similar-looking option names can describe different contracts.

Record underlying, call or put, strike, and expiration. Also check the **premium multiplier** and **deliverable**—what exercise transfers—as separate fields. An adjustment can change the deliverable while leaving the premium multiplier unchanged. Do not guess about an unfamiliar contract. [OIC: contract adjustments after splits](https://www.optionseducation.org/news/splits-happen).

**Worked example:** “ABC call, $50 strike, Friday A expiration” and “ABC call, $50 strike, Friday B expiration” are different contracts because the expirations differ. If a display says only “ABC $50,” the option type, expiration, multiplier, and deliverable remain unknown; there is no complete dollar calculation to trust yet.

**Try it:** A screen shows “ABC Friday A $45 put, premium $1.10” but hides the multiplier and deliverable. Can you confidently calculate the contract's premium dollars and exercise share quantity? What is missing?

<details>
<summary>Answer — open after your attempt</summary>

No. The premium multiplier is needed to convert the quote into dollars, and the deliverable is needed to know what exercise transfers. Check the exact series' contract specification and any applicable OCC adjustment memo.

</details>

lessons.title: selling an owned option differs from writing a new one
lessons.body:
**Time: 5–10 minutes. One idea:** track whether an action opens or closes a position.

**Long** means you own the option. **Short** means you have written it and carry its obligation. Buying to open creates a long option; selling to close removes an owned option. Selling to open creates a short option; buying to close removes it. Selling does not always mean opening a new obligation. These words describe the option position, not simply a bullish or bearish view. [FINRA: opening long and short options positions](https://www.finra.org/investors/insights/trading-options-understanding-assignment).

**Worked example:** You own 1 ABC call. Sell **that same contract** to close, and your quantity goes `+1 − 1 = 0`. Start at zero and sell 1 to open instead, and your quantity becomes `−1`: a short call with obligations.

**Try it:** You own 2 ABC puts and sell both identical puts to close. What option quantity remains? Did this action itself create a short put position?

<details>
<summary>Answer — open after your attempt</summary>

`+2 − 2 = 0`; no puts remain. This closing sale did not create a short put position. Selling additional contracts beyond the owned quantity would be a different situation.

</details>

checkpoint:
## Checkpoint 2: read the contract carefully

Use standard 100-share stock options with multiplier 100, ignoring fees, except when fields are explicitly missing.

1. **Safety:** What right does one $32 call give its buyer, and what strike payment does exercise require?
2. **Safety:** A holder owns 100 shares and exercises one $28 put. State the share and strike-cash flows.
3. **Safety:** You buy 3 options quoted at $0.70 each with multiplier 100. What premium dollars are paid? Is that also the strike payment for shares?
4. A Friday A $40 call and Friday B $40 call have the same underlying. Are they identical contracts? Why?
5. **Safety:** You own 1 call and sell the same call to close. What remains? If a different chain hides its multiplier and adjusted deliverable, may you assume they are both 100?

<details>
<summary>Checkpoint 2 worked key — open after all five attempts</summary>

1. Right to buy 100 shares at $32 each under the terms; strike payment `100 × $32 = $3,200`.
2. Deliver 100 shares and receive `100 × $28 = $2,800`. Premium was a separate earlier cash flow.
3. `3 × $0.70 × 100 = $210`. This pays for the options. Any exercise share purchase uses separate strike cash.
4. No. Different expirations mean different contracts, even if the underlying and strike match.
5. Quantity becomes `+1 − 1 = 0`. No option remains from that position. No, hidden contract terms must be verified; adjusted contracts can have different deliverables.

</details>

**Pass rule:** all five correct, with every safety answer and unit explained without notes. On a miss, correct the reasoning, then have a tutor change the numbers or contract identity and attempt that fresh version before seeing its key. Proceed once all are correct. This is an educational checkpoint.

title: Understand profit and loss
description: Separate an option’s value from the money you made.
introduction:
[Previous: option contracts](beginner/02_CONTRACTS.md) · [Course home](README.md) · [Next: changing option prices](beginner/04_PRICES.md)

Take one 5–10 minute lesson per session. All examples use fictional ABC, one **standard 100-share stock option**, multiplier 100, and **ignore fees and taxes**. Unless explicitly closing early, the arithmetic is an idealized **expiration** calculation: assume intrinsic value is realized. Actual stock-option exercise transfers shares and strike cash; it does not simply deposit the profit shown here. Study [operations](beginner/05_OPERATIONS.md) before any simulation that includes expiration.

lessons.title: a call's intrinsic value is its favorable exercise difference
lessons.body:
**Time: 5–10 minutes. One idea:** a call's intrinsic value comes from buying below the stock's market price.

For a standard call, subtract strike from stock price. If the result is negative, use zero. This is **intrinsic value**, not yet profit and not necessarily the option's market price before expiration. [OIC: options pricing](https://www.optionseducation.org/optionsoverview/options-pricing).

**Worked example:** ABC is $34 and a call's strike is $30. The favorable difference is `$34 − $30 = $4` per share, or `$4 × 100 = $400` per contract. If ABC were $28, buying at $30 would give no favorable difference; intrinsic value would be $0, not negative $200.

**Try it:** At expiration ABC is $47 and a standard call's strike is $44. What is the call's intrinsic value per share and per contract?

<details>
<summary>Answer — open after your attempt</summary>

Per share: `$47 − $44 = $3`. Per contract: `$3 × 100 = $300`. This number has not yet subtracted what the buyer paid for the option.

</details>

lessons.title: call profit subtracts the premium
lessons.body:
**Time: 5–10 minutes. One idea:** a valuable call can still lose money for its buyer.

At expiration, the call buyer's idealized result is `intrinsic value in dollars − premium dollars paid`. A negative answer is a loss. Losing the full option premium is possible. This describes the option's economics; a stock position produced by exercise introduces its own exposure. [OIC: long-call risk and profit](https://www.optionseducation.org/strategies/all-strategies/long-call).

**Worked example:** Buy a $30 call for $2 quoted premium: cost `$2 × 100 = $200`. ABC finishes at $31. Intrinsic value is `($31 − $30) × 100 = $100`. Profit is `$100 − $200 = −$100`. The stock ending above the strike did not cover the premium.

**Try it:** Buy a $40 call for $1.50. ABC finishes at $43. What are premium dollars, expiration intrinsic value, and profit before fees?

<details>
<summary>Answer — open after your attempt</summary>

Premium `$1.50 × 100 = $150`; intrinsic `($43 − $40) × 100 = $300`; profit `$300 − $150 = $150`. At or below $40, the idealized option result would instead lose the full $150 premium.

</details>

lessons.title: a put's intrinsic value comes from selling above market
lessons.body:
**Time: 5–10 minutes. One idea:** reverse the subtraction for a put.

A put provides a sale right, so subtract stock price from strike. Use zero if that difference is negative. A put with a higher strike than stock price has favorable exercise value. [OIC: put value](https://www.optionseducation.org/optionsoverview/options-pricing).

**Worked example:** ABC is $26 and a put's strike is $30. Selling at $30 rather than $26 gives a `$30 − $26 = $4` difference per share. Intrinsic value is `$4 × 100 = $400`. At stock $33, the $30 sale right has $0 intrinsic value.

**Try it:** ABC finishes at $52 and a standard put's strike is $57. Calculate intrinsic value per share and per contract.

<details>
<summary>Answer — open after your attempt</summary>

`$57 − $52 = $5` per share; `$5 × 100 = $500` per contract. Strike minus stock is the put subtraction. Stock minus strike would reverse the economic meaning.

</details>

lessons.title: put profit also subtracts the premium
lessons.body:
**Time: 5–10 minutes. One idea:** the price of the put must be recovered before its buyer profits.

At expiration, the put buyer's idealized profit is `intrinsic value in dollars − premium dollars paid`. The stock falling does not guarantee enough put value to cover the purchase cost. The entire option premium can be lost. [OIC: long-put risk and profit](https://www.optionseducation.org/strategies/all-strategies/long-put).

**Worked example:** Buy a $50 put for $3: cost `$3 × 100 = $300`. ABC finishes at $48. Intrinsic value is `($50 − $48) × 100 = $200`. The result is `$200 − $300 = −$100`, despite the put having intrinsic value.

**Try it:** Buy a $35 put for $1.20. ABC finishes at $32. Find premium dollars, intrinsic value, and expiration profit before fees.

<details>
<summary>Answer — open after your attempt</summary>

Premium: `$1.20 × 100 = $120`. Intrinsic: `($35 − $32) × 100 = $300`. Profit: `$300 − $120 = $180`. At or above $35, the idealized option result loses the full $120 premium.

</details>

lessons.title: expiration break-even is one specific calculation
lessons.body:
**Time: 5–10 minutes. One idea:** expiration break-even does not dictate a profitable early sale.

Before fees, a purchased call breaks even **at expiration** at `strike + premium`; a purchased put at `strike − premium`. Before expiration you may sell the owned option to close. Then compare actual sale proceeds with its purchase cost and fees. A changing market price includes more than intrinsic value. [SEC: options introduction](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins-63).

**Worked example:** A $50 call bought for $2 has $52 expiration break-even. Suppose ABC is $51 before expiration and you actually sell the call at $2.60. Sale proceeds `$260` minus purchase `$200` give `$60` profit before fees. ABC did not need to reach $52 for this early sale to profit. The $2.60 fill is an assumption, not a promise.

**Try it:** A $40 put costs $1.50. Find its expiration break-even. If you instead close it early at an actual $1.90 sale price, what is the profit before fees?

<details>
<summary>Answer — open after your attempt</summary>

Expiration break-even: `$40 − $1.50 = $38.50`. Early sale profit: `($1.90 − $1.50) × 100 = $40`. The early result uses actual option prices, not the expiration formula.

</details>

lessons.title: “in the money” describes the contract, not your profit
lessons.body:
**Time: 5–10 minutes. One idea:** moneyness compares stock and strike only.

A call is **in the money** when stock is above strike; a put when stock is below strike. At the strike is **at the money**; the unfavorable side is **out of the money**. These labels do not subtract your premium. [OIC: basic option terms](https://www.optionseducation.org/optionsoverview/options-basics).

**Worked example:** A $20 call bought for $2 finishes with ABC at $21. It is in the money by $1 per share. Its idealized expiration result is `(1 − 2) × 100 = −$100`. “In the money” and “profitable” therefore answer different questions.

**Try it:** A $60 put bought for $4 expires with ABC at $58. Is it in, at, or out of the money? What is the buyer's idealized profit before fees?

<details>
<summary>Answer — open after your attempt</summary>

In the money: stock $58 is below put strike $60. Intrinsic is `$2 × 100 = $200`. Subtract `$4 × 100 = $400` premium for a `$200` loss. Moneyness alone did not establish profit.

</details>

lessons.title: an uncovered short call has no finite loss ceiling
lessons.body:
**Time: 5–10 minutes. One idea:** premium received does not cap a writer's loss.

An **uncovered short call** means a written call without offsetting shares or another protective position. If assigned, its writer must deliver shares at the strike. A stock has no fixed upper price ceiling, so the call writer's theoretical loss has no finite maximum. This is a risk-recognition exercise. [OIC: uncovered call](https://www.optionseducation.org/strategies/all-strategies/naked-call-uncovered-call-short-call).

**Worked example:** Write one $50 call for $1: receive `$100`. ABC finishes at $60. Its favorable value to the holder is `($60 − $50) × 100 = $1,000`, an obligation for the writer. The writer's idealized result is `$100 − $1,000 = −$900`. At still higher stock prices, losses keep increasing.

**Try it:** An uncovered $70 call is written for $2. ABC finishes at $80. What is idealized expiration profit or loss before fees? Is that the maximum possible loss?

<details>
<summary>Answer — open after your attempt</summary>

Premium `$200`; intrinsic obligation `($80 − $70) × 100 = $1,000`; result `$200 − $1,000 = −$800`. No, $800 is this scenario's loss. The theoretical loss has no finite ceiling as stock price rises.

</details>

lessons.title: a short put can require a large share purchase
lessons.body:
**Time: 5–10 minutes. One idea:** distinguish premium received from the purchase obligation.

If assigned on a standard stock put, its writer buys 100 shares at the strike. Cash set aside for that purchase does not prevent the stock from losing value. Assuming stock cannot fall below zero, the short put's greatest idealized expiration loss is `strike × 100 − premium dollars received`, before fees. [OIC: cash-secured put](https://www.optionseducation.org/strategies/all-strategies/cash-secured-put).

**Worked example:** Write a $40 put for $1: receive `$100`. If assigned, pay `$40 × 100 = $4,000` and receive 100 shares. If they are worth zero, the modeled loss is `$4,000 − $100 = $3,900`. The premium was $100; the potential loss was much larger.

**Try it:** Write a $25 put for $0.80. State the premium received, assigned share purchase payment, shares received, and greatest idealized expiration loss before fees.

<details>
<summary>Answer — open after your attempt</summary>

Premium: `$0.80 × 100 = $80`. If assigned: pay `$25 × 100 = $2,500`, receive 100 shares. At stock zero, loss is `$2,500 − $80 = $2,420`. Receiving $80 did not reduce the strike payment to $80.

</details>

checkpoint:
## Checkpoint 3: separate value, profit, and obligations

Use one standard contract, multiplier 100, no fees or taxes. Values are idealized expiration values unless stated otherwise.

1. Buy a $55 call for $2.20. ABC finishes at $59. Find premium dollars, intrinsic value, and profit.
2. Buy a $70 put for $3. ABC finishes at $68. Find intrinsic value, profit, moneyness, and expiration break-even.
3. A $30 call bought for $1.40 is sold to close **before expiration** at an actual $1.75. Find the early-sale profit and the separate expiration break-even stock price.
4. **Safety:** Write an uncovered $45 call for $1.50. ABC finishes at $52. Find the modeled result and state whether the theoretical loss has a finite ceiling.
5. **Safety:** Write a $38 put for $1.10. State assigned shares and strike cash; calculate greatest idealized expiration loss at stock zero. Does holding enough cash remove that price risk?

<details>
<summary>Checkpoint 3 worked key — open after all five attempts</summary>

1. Premium `$2.20 × 100 = $220`; intrinsic `($59 − $55) × 100 = $400`; profit `$400 − $220 = $180`.
2. Intrinsic `($70 − $68) × 100 = $200`; premium `$300`; profit `−$100`. The put is in the money, yet unprofitable. Expiration break-even `$70 − $3 = $67`.
3. Sale profit `($1.75 − $1.40) × 100 = $35`. Expiration break-even is separately `$30 + $1.40 = $31.40`. It is not a stock-price requirement for that completed early sale.
4. Premium `$150` less intrinsic obligation `($52 − $45) × 100 = $700` gives `−$550`. An uncovered short call has no finite theoretical loss ceiling.
5. If assigned, pay `$38 × 100 = $3,800` and receive 100 shares. Greatest idealized expiration loss is `$3,800 − $110 = $3,690`. Cash can fund the purchase; it does not keep the shares from falling.

</details>

**Pass rule:** all five correct with units and reasoning; both safety items must be explained without prompts. For any miss, correct the error and solve a changed-number version supplied by your tutor before seeing its answer. Advance once all five are correct. These calculations do not establish live-trading readiness.

title: Why option prices change
description: Explore time, volatility and the Greeks, one at a time.
introduction:
[Course home](beginner/README.md) · [Previous: profit and loss](beginner/03_PROFIT.md) · [Next: operations](beginner/05_OPERATIONS.md) · [Full library](README.md)

**Lessons 25–32.** Take one lesson per study day: about 5–10 minutes to read, work the example, and answer; then 3–5 minutes to recall yesterday's idea. These are fictional standard stock/ETF options with a **100 multiplier**. Fees are **$0 for teaching arithmetic** throughout this module; actual trading includes fees and bid/ask costs. A model estimate is not a tradable price.

Your goal: explain why a correct guess about stock direction can still lose money. You do not need a pricing formula or coding.

lessons.title: Today's sale price and expiration value are different
lessons.body:
Before expiration, you may sell an option you own if a buyer is available. Your result then depends on the actual sale price. You do not have to exercise it or wait until its last day. At expiration, the simple payoff calculations from Module 3 use the stock price and strike; before then, remaining time and market conditions also affect the option's price. [SEC's introduction explains selling, exercising, and expiration](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins-63).

**Worked example:** Buy a $50 call for $2.00: pay $200. A week later, with time remaining, you sell at an actual $2.60 fill: receive $260. Profit is **$60**. You do not need the stock above the $52 *expiration* break-even to sell the option profitably before expiration. The sale price is what matters to this closed trade.

**Try it:** Buy one option for $1.80 and sell it before expiration for $1.45. What is the result? What extra information would you need to value a different option still open?

<details><summary>Check your reasoning</summary>

`(1.45 − 1.80) × 100 = −$35`. For an open option, the current executable bid/ask and contract details matter; its expiration break-even alone cannot tell you today's value.

</details>

**Recall:** Which price determines a closed option trade's sale proceeds?

lessons.title: Extrinsic value is the part beyond immediate exercise value
lessons.body:
**Intrinsic value** is the option's immediate exercise value per share: for a call, stock minus strike if positive; for a put, strike minus stock if positive. Otherwise it is zero. **Extrinsic value**, sometimes called time value, is the option premium minus intrinsic value. It reflects the remaining possibilities and other pricing inputs, rather than a separate cash payment. Use coherent, current quotes; stale or wide markets can make this decomposition misleading. [OIC explains intrinsic and time value](https://www.optionseducation.org/optionsoverview/options-pricing).

**Worked example:** Stock is $54. A $50 call trades for $5.20. Intrinsic value is `$54 − $50 = $4`; extrinsic value is `$5.20 − $4 = $1.20`. The contract premium is **$520**, consisting of **$400 intrinsic** and **$120 extrinsic**. These parts are values, not profit: you still compare with what you paid.

**Try it:** Stock is $47. A $50 put has a $4 premium. Find intrinsic and extrinsic value per share and per contract.

<details><summary>Check your reasoning</summary>

Put intrinsic value is `50 − 47 = $3/share`, or $300. Extrinsic is `4 − 3 = $1/share`, or $100. Total premium is $400. A put gains immediate exercise value when stock is below its strike.

</details>

**Recall:** Can an option with zero intrinsic value still have a sale price before expiration? Explain why.

lessons.title: Theta describes one effect of time passing
lessons.body:
An option has a deadline. With everything else held fixed, a purchased plain option commonly loses value as time passes. **Theta** is a model estimate of that time effect. Many platforms show it per calendar day, but you must check the platform's units. It is not a fee collected daily, and it does not promise tomorrow's price. Some options and conditions have different signs; learn the convention before using a number. [OIC's theta lesson explains time sensitivity](https://www.optionseducation.org/advancedconcepts/theta).

**Worked example:** A long call is valued at $2.00 and its displayed theta is **−$0.03 per share per day**. Holding the model's other inputs unchanged, the one-day estimate is `$2.00 − $0.03 = $1.97`, or **$3 less per contract**. If the stock rises strongly, the option can gain despite that time effect. Theta also changes; multiplying today's value by 30 is not a reliable month forecast.

**Try it:** A long put's theta is −$0.04/share/day. What is the time-only estimate for one standard contract over one day? Does it determine the full day's profit?

<details><summary>Check your reasoning</summary>

`−0.04 × 100 = −$4`. No. Stock price, implied volatility, rates, dividends, changing sensitivities, and the market's bid/ask can change the result.

</details>

**Recall:** Why is positive theta on a short position not guaranteed daily income?

lessons.title: Realized volatility looks backward; implied volatility comes from price
lessons.body:
**Volatility** describes the size and variability of price movement, rather than simply whether price rose or fell. **Realized volatility** summarizes movement already observed over a stated period. **Implied volatility (IV)** is the volatility input that makes a pricing model match an observed option price. IV reflects market pricing under a model, including demand and compensation for risk. It is not a promised future movement. [OIC distinguishes historical and implied volatility](https://www.optionseducation.org/advancedconcepts/volatility-the-greeks).

**Worked example:** A platform reports a stock's past 30-day realized volatility as 18% and one option's IV as 28%, both annualized. You can say **28% is 10 percentage points above 18%**. You cannot conclude the option is overpriced: the next month may include an event that the previous month did not. Different strikes and expirations can have different IVs.

**Try it:** Past realized volatility is 20% and an option's IV is 30%. Is that a 10 percentage-point gap or a 10% proportional increase? Does it establish a profitable selling opportunity?

<details><summary>Check your reasoning</summary>

It is **10 percentage points**. The proportional increase from 20 to 30 is 50%. Neither number proves future profit; the future movement, contract terms, prices, costs, and risks are still unknown.

</details>

**Recall:** Which measure comes from past movement, and which is backed out of an option quote?

lessons.title: Delta estimates a small stock-price effect
lessons.body:
**Delta** estimates how much an option's value changes for a $1 stock move, with other model inputs fixed. A long call usually has positive delta; a long put usually has negative delta. A short position reverses the corresponding long option's sign. Delta changes as conditions change. It is not a guaranteed probability of profit. [OIC's delta explanation gives the units and limitations](https://www.optionseducation.org/advancedconcepts/delta).

**Worked example:** One long call has delta +0.40. For a small **$0.50 stock rise**, the delta-only estimate is `0.40 × $0.50 = +$0.20/share`, or **+$20 per contract**. This is a value-change estimate, not final profit; your entry cost, other changing inputs, fees, and actual sale price still matter.

**Try it:** One long put has delta −0.30. For a small $1 stock decline, what is its delta-only value change per share and contract?

<details><summary>Check your reasoning</summary>

`−0.30 × −$1 = +$0.30/share`, or **+$30 per contract**. Both signs are negative in the multiplication, producing a positive estimate. This assumes the delta remains sufficiently stable and other inputs do not change.

</details>

**Recall:** What must you multiply a per-share delta estimate by to get one standard contract's dollar estimate?

lessons.title: Gamma explains why delta changes
lessons.body:
Delta is a snapshot. **Gamma** estimates how much delta changes for a $1 stock move, with other inputs fixed. This is why a straight-line delta estimate becomes less reliable over a large move. Long plain calls and puts generally have positive gamma; short positions have the opposite exposure. You only need that idea today. [OIC explains gamma](https://www.optionseducation.org/advancedconcepts/gamma).

**Worked example:** A long call starts with delta +0.50 and gamma +0.04 per $1. After a small $1 stock rise, its new delta might be approximately `0.50 + 0.04 = 0.54`. After a small $1 decline, it might be `0.50 − 0.04 = 0.46`. These are new **delta readings**, not option premiums or profits. Near expiration, certain options can change exposure quickly, especially near the strike.

**Try it:** A call has delta +0.35 and gamma +0.03. Estimate its new delta after a $1 rise. Why should you avoid applying that same arithmetic to a $20 overnight jump as if it were exact?

<details><summary>Check your reasoning</summary>

Approximately **+0.38**. Over a large jump, gamma itself and the other inputs can change substantially; a local approximation cannot promise the new delta or price.

</details>

**Recall:** Does a position's current delta stay fixed until expiration?

lessons.title: Vega and rho measure two other inputs
lessons.body:
Two more labels appear on option screens. **Vega** commonly estimates the per-share value change for a **one percentage-point IV change**, such as 25% to 26%. **Rho** commonly estimates the value change for a **one percentage-point interest-rate change**. Check the platform's units. For now, recognize the labels; you need not predict interest rates or memorize every sign. [OIC lists the five Greeks](https://www.optionseducation.org/advancedconcepts/volatility-the-greeks).

**Worked example:** A long call has vega +$0.08/share per IV point. IV rises from 25% to 27%: two points. Its vega-only estimate is `0.08 × 2 × 100 = +$16`. Separately, if rho is +$0.05/share per rate point and the rate rises from 4% to 5%, the rho-only estimate is **+$5 per contract**. Neither estimate includes the other moving inputs. Plain long calls and puts generally benefit from higher IV under otherwise fixed model inputs.

**Try it:** One long option has vega +$0.12/share/IV point. IV falls from 30% to 28%. What is the vega-only dollar effect?

<details><summary>Check your reasoning</summary>

The change is **−2 IV points**. `0.12 × (−2) × 100 = −$24`. Do not multiply by 2% of the premium; the stated unit already tells you the calculation.

</details>

**Recall:** What is the difference between a percentage point and a percentage change?

lessons.title: An earnings event can remove uncertainty and lower option value
lessons.body:
An **earnings announcement** is a company's report of financial results. Before it arrives, option prices can include substantial uncertainty about the stock's reaction. After the news, IV may fall sharply, sometimes called **IV crush**. A call can lose money even when the stock rises, because the favorable move may not offset the IV fall, time passage, and trading costs. This is a possible outcome, not an automatic rule around every announcement. [OIC explains how volatility affects option prices](https://www.optionseducation.org/advancedconcepts/vega).

**Worked example:** Buy a call for $4 before an announcement: pay $400. The next day the stock is slightly higher, but the option's actual sale fill is $3.20. The closed trade loses `(3.20 − 4.00) × 100 = −$80`. Without full market and model inputs, you cannot attribute all $80 to IV alone. Direction was one part of the result.

**Try it:** A put costs $3 before news. The stock falls slightly, but the actual option sale price afterward is $2.40. What is the result, and what mistaken belief does it challenge?

<details><summary>Check your reasoning</summary>

`(2.40 − 3.00) × 100 = −$60`. A correct directional guess does not guarantee profit on a purchased option. Check the magnitude and timing of the move, IV, time left, and bid/ask.

</details>

**Recall:** Name two variables besides stock direction that affect an option before expiration.

1. Buy a call for $2.20 and sell before expiration for $2.65. Calculate one standard contract's result. Is its expiration break-even needed for that calculation?
2. Stock is $62. A $60 call trades for $3.50. Find intrinsic and extrinsic value per share and contract.
3. A long put has delta −0.40 and the stock falls $0.50. Estimate the delta-only change for one contract. Then explain why it is not a promised sale price.
4. Vega is +$0.10/share/IV point. IV falls from 32% to 29%. Calculate the vega-only contract change. Is IV a guaranteed forecast of future realized movement?

<details><summary>Checkpoint worked key · open after saving your answers</summary>

1. `(2.65 − 2.20) × 100 = +$45`, with $0 teaching fees. No: the completed trade uses actual buy and sell prices.
2. Intrinsic `62 − 60 = $2/share`, **$200/contract**. Extrinsic `3.50 − 2 = $1.50/share`, **$150/contract**. Total is $350; value is not profit.
3. `−0.40 × −0.50 × 100 = +$20`. Other inputs and delta can change; bid/ask and execution determine the sale price.
4. `0.10 × (−3) × 100 = −$30`. No: IV is a model input inferred from current option price, not a promise.
5. IV may fall, time passes, and spread/fees can outweigh a favorable direction. Theta is local and changes with the option's state; it is not a fixed daily bill.

</details>

**Pass and retry:** Answer all five correctly and explain the units aloud. For any miss, record the mistaken idea, repeat that lesson, then solve a changed-number version without the key on your next study day. These are learning checks, not proof of trading readiness. Do one minute of recall on this module after 1, 3, and 7 study days.

title: Exercise and expiration
description: Follow the shares and cash through the life of a contract.
introduction:
[Course home](beginner/README.md) · [Previous: prices](beginner/04_PRICES.md) · [Next: strategies](beginner/06_STRATEGIES.md) · [Full library](README.md)

**Lessons 33–40.** Study one lesson a day, then spend 3–5 minutes recalling an earlier lesson. Unless a lesson explicitly changes the product, every example is a fictional **American-style stock/ETF option delivering 100 shares with a 100 premium multiplier**. Fees, interest, taxes, borrowing costs, and dividends are **$0 in the arithmetic**, except the dividend stated in Lesson 38. Actual account treatment must be checked with the broker.

Your goal: show the cash, shares, options, and order status after an event. The [OCC disclosure document](https://www.theocc.com/company-information/documents-and-archives/options-disclosure-document) is the official reference; read its relevant sections as these terms become familiar and before any real options trading.

lessons.title: Opening and closing create four different actions
lessons.body:
An option order includes whether it **opens** or **closes** a position. Buying does not always start a bullish bet, and selling does not always open a short position. Use the exact same option series—underlying, type, strike, expiration, and deliverable—when closing it. [SEC explains closing transactions](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins-63).

| Action | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| Buy to open | Creates a long option you own |
| Sell to close | Removes an existing long option |
| Sell to open | Creates a short option obligation |
| Buy to close | Removes an existing short option |

**Worked example:** Starting with no options, buy to open one call at $2: cash falls $200, position is **+1 call**. Later sell to close that same call at $2.30: cash rises $230, position becomes **0**, and profit is **$30**. Selling a different expiration would leave two separate positions rather than closing the first.

**Try it:** You sold to open one put for $1.50. Which action closes it if the actual repurchase price is $2? What is the result?

<details><summary>Check your reasoning</summary>

**Buy to close** the same put series. Entry +$150, closing −$200, net **−$50**. A submitted order removes no position until the required closing fill is confirmed.

</details>

**Recall:** Which sale creates an obligation and which sale removes an asset?

lessons.title: Exercise uses the contract; closing sells the contract
lessons.body:
**Exercising** a physically settled call uses its right to buy shares at the strike. Exercising a put uses its right to sell shares at the strike. This is different from selling the option. An option premium is paid separately from the exercise amount. [OIC explains exercise cash and share delivery](https://www.optionseducation.org/optionsoverview/exercising-options).

**Worked example:** You paid $2 for one $50 call: **$200 premium**. Exercising requires **$5,000** to buy **100 shares** at $50. It removes the call and creates the stock position. If the stock is $54, the shares are worth $5,400 at that reference price; the gain after premium is $200 before excluded costs. Cash required to exercise is much greater than the $200 premium. A later stock fall can create additional stock losses.

Selling an option with remaining extrinsic value can preserve value that exercise would discard, if a suitable sale can be executed. The best available action depends on actual quotes, deadlines, and the account.

**Try it:** One long $40 put is exercised while the holder owns the required 100 shares. What shares and cash move? What happens to the option?

<details><summary>Check your reasoning</summary>

The holder delivers **100 shares**, receives **$4,000**, and the put ceases to be open. The earlier premium is a separate cash flow. Without the shares, exercise may create short stock if permitted, or prompt broker intervention; verify account rules.

</details>

**Recall:** Does a $200 call premium mean only $200 is needed to exercise it?

lessons.title: Assignment can arrive before expiration
lessons.body:
**Assignment** means a short option writer must fulfill an exercised contract. An American-style short option can be assigned on any business day while open. You cannot guarantee which day or predict the assigned account. A protective long option in a spread does not automatically exercise to fix the short leg's obligation. [FINRA explains early and one-leg assignment](https://www.finra.org/investors/insights/trading-options-understanding-assignment).

**Worked example:** Sell one $45 put for $1. You receive **$100 premium**. If assigned, you pay **$4,500** and receive **100 shares**. The short put disappears, but the shares remain. At a $40 stock reference price they are worth $4,000, so the position's result including the initial premium is **−$400**. Cash received initially was not guaranteed profit.

If a call is assigned, the writer must deliver shares instead. Without owned shares, permitted assignment can create short stock, whose losses grow as stock rises. A broker can require funds or liquidate positions under its rules.

**Try it:** One short $60 call is assigned. The writer already owns 100 shares. What are the resulting share and cash changes? Does the writer choose to decline assignment?

<details><summary>Check your reasoning</summary>

Deliver **100 shares**, receive **$6,000**, remove the short call. The writer cannot decline a valid assignment because the outcome is inconvenient. Include the original stock cost and option premium when calculating total profit.

</details>

**Recall:** Is the long leg of a spread an automatic instruction to resolve assignment?

lessons.title: American and European describe exercise timing
lessons.body:
**American-style** options permit exercise before expiration within the applicable rules. **European-style** options permit exercise only at their specified expiration exercise time. These labels describe contract rights, not the country where you live or trade. Exercise style and settlement type are separate fields. U.S. stock and ETF options are generally American-style and physically settled; many index products have different terms. [OIC compares equity and index options](https://www.optionseducation.org/advancedconcepts/equity-vs-index-options).

**Worked example:** Two fictional calls both have 20 days remaining and a $100 strike. Stock/index reference is 105. The American-style holder may exercise now under its rules; the European-style holder cannot exercise now just because it has five points of intrinsic value. Either might be sold before expiry if a suitable market is available. A sale is not early exercise.

**Try it:** A European-style option has 10 days remaining and five points of intrinsic value. Does that permit immediate exercise? Does it prevent the holder from trying to sell the option?

<details><summary>Check your reasoning</summary>

No immediate exercise: its exercise timing is restricted. It can generally be traded before expiry during its trading hours, subject to market availability. The word European does not mean you must hold until expiration.

</details>

**Recall:** Name the two different questions answered by exercise style and settlement type.

lessons.title: Expiration can create a stock position automatically
lessons.body:
For standard U.S. equity options, OCC's **exercise-by-exception** procedure generally exercises expiring options at least **$0.01 in the money**, absent contrary instructions through the clearing member. Broker procedures, deadlines, buying power, and product rules matter. A broker may close a position or submit different instructions under its policies. Do not assume doing nothing avoids a share obligation. [OIC's exercise FAQ explains the threshold and exceptions](https://www.optionseducation.org/referencelibrary/faq/options-exercise).

**Worked example:** One $50 call reaches expiration with the relevant stock close at $50.05. Its exercise value is only **$5**, but exercise buys **100 shares for $5,000**. Those shares can move sharply afterward. Conversely, an option out of the money at the close can still be exercised under valid instructions after an after-hours move; the close does not settle every assignment question. [FINRA illustrates after-hours spread risk](https://www.finra.org/investors/insights/trading-options-understanding-assignment).

**Try it:** A long $70 call is $0.02 in the money at expiration. Under the standard procedure and no contrary instruction, what purchase may occur? Why is the $2 intrinsic value a misleading measure of the resulting cash requirement?

<details><summary>Check your reasoning</summary>

Exercise may buy **100 shares for $7,000**. The $2 is `0.02 × 100` immediate exercise value, not purchase funding or a limit on later stock losses. Confirm the broker's actual exercise and liquidation policy in advance.

</details>

**Recall:** Does submitting a closing order guarantee that an expiring position is gone?

lessons.title: A dividend can change early-call assignment incentives
lessons.body:
A **dividend** is a distribution by a company or fund. The **ex-dividend date** determines whether a new stock buyer is entitled to that distribution under the applicable rules. A call holder does not receive the stock dividend just for owning a call. Approaching that date, early exercise of certain in-the-money calls may become more attractive, increasing assignment risk for short calls. [OIC describes dividends and early exercise](https://www.optionseducation.org/optionsoverview/exercising-options).

**Worked example:** Stock is $52. An open $50 call has an observed premium of $2.10: $2 intrinsic plus $0.10 extrinsic. An upcoming dividend is $0.60/share. The dividend exceeds that $0.10 of remaining extrinsic value, making early exercise worth investigating for a holder, subject to financing, quotes, and other details. It does not prove assignment will happen.

If assignment leaves a writer short 100 shares across the ex-date, the account may owe a **$60 dividend-related payment**, in addition to stock-price and borrowing consequences. A covered writer may instead lose the owned shares and the expected dividend.

**Try it:** A short call is open before an ex-date. Assignment leaves 100 shares short, and the stated dividend is $0.40/share. What potential dividend-related cash obligation must be included?

<details><summary>Check your reasoning</summary>

**$40**, under the stated 100-share short and dividend assumption. Stock-price changes are separate; a stock typically adjusts around its dividend, so the payment alone is not the full economic result. Verify broker handling.

</details>

**Recall:** Does owning a call by itself entitle you to a stock dividend?

lessons.title: Multiplier, deliverable, and settlement are separate fields
lessons.body:
Do not let the familiar number 100 replace the contract specification. The **premium multiplier** converts a quote to dollars. The **deliverable** states what changes hands on exercise. **Settlement** can involve shares or a cash amount. Corporate actions can create adjusted contracts with unusual deliverables. [OCC's disclosure reference](https://www.theocc.com/company-information/documents-and-archives/options-disclosure-document) and [adjustment memos](https://infomemo.theocc.com/infomemo/search-memo) describe the actual terms.

**Worked example:** A fictional cash-settled index call has strike 5,000, premium 15 index points, and a $100 multiplier. It costs **$1,500**. If its official settlement value is 5,020, it pays **$2,000 cash**, producing $500 before costs and **no shares**. The official settlement value can differ from the last displayed index value; A.M. and P.M. series differ. [Cboe specifies its index products](https://www.cboe.com/tradable_products/sp_500/spx_weekly_options/specifications).

An adjusted stock option might retain a 100 premium multiplier but deliver only 10 shares after a reverse split. This is a separate contract feature, not a cash-settlement rule. [OIC gives a reverse-split example](https://www.optionseducation.org/news/splits-happen).

**Try it:** A memo-confirmed adjusted contract has quoted premium $2, a 100 premium multiplier, and a 10-share deliverable. Is its premium $20 or $200? Can you infer the exercise cash payment from “10 shares” alone?

<details><summary>Check your reasoning</summary>

Premium is **$200**. You need the memo's strike/exercise terms to determine exercise cash; deliverable count alone is insufficient. Do not silently treat it as an ordinary contract.

</details>

**Recall:** Which field converts a premium quote to dollars?

lessons.title: Read a chain and rehearse an order ticket
lessons.body:
An **option chain** groups contracts by expiration and strike. First select the exact series; then read its bid/ask and timestamp. Volume counts trading activity; open interest counts outstanding contracts. Neither guarantees a fill. A chain's “last” trade can be stale. [OIC's basics FAQ explains quote fields](https://www.optionseducation.org/referencelibrary/faq/basics).

**Worked example:** A fictional chain row is **ABC · 30 days left · $50 call · $1.90 bid / $2.10 ask · size 4/2 · last $2.30**. ABC is an invented symbol. The standard 100 multiplier makes the displayed ask **$210/contract**. The $20 spread is `(2.10 − 1.90) × 100`. The last $2.30 is not today's offered buy price. A learning ticket could say **buy to open 1, $2.00 limit, day order**; it may never fill because its limit is below the displayed ask. Size can disappear as quotes change.

Before a real ticket, verify the actual expiration date, contract identifier, deliverable, events, permitted strategy, total costs, funding, and exit/expiry plan. Here, write **“simulation only; no order submitted.”** A paper fill also has limitations. [IBKR documents simulated fills](https://www.ibkrguides.com/orgportal/aboutpapertradingaccount.htm).

**Try it:** A row shows $1.40 bid/$1.70 ask, 100 multiplier. You own one option and write a sell-to-close limit of $1.60. What proceeds would a fill at exactly that limit produce? Does the visible quote establish a fill?

<details><summary>Check your reasoning</summary>

**$160 before fees** if filled at exactly $1.60. No: the displayed bid is $1.40, and even a later quote cannot replace an execution confirmation. Preserve the order ID and status in a simulation or actual account record.

</details>

**Recall:** What evidence tells you an order actually executed?

Confirm product terms, funding, exercise/do-not-exercise deadline, and broker liquidation procedures. Do not assume the broker guarantees this particular outcome.
4. **No.** Reconcile delivered or short shares, assignment cash, remaining option, buying power, pending orders, and broker deadlines. A spread diagram is not an automatic account workflow.

title: Understand the strategies
description: Understand common positions and the choice to make no trade.
introduction:
[Course home](beginner/README.md) · [Previous: operations](beginner/05_OPERATIONS.md) · [Next: risk](beginner/07_RISK.md) · [Full library](README.md)

**Lessons 41–48.** These structures are for understanding and simulation. Knowing their names is not a recommendation to use them. Study one lesson a day; use the remaining 3–5 minutes to redraw yesterday's cash flows.

Every worked example uses fictional **100-share standard American-style stock/ETF options**. Stock and option quantities are stated. All option legs of a spread have the **same underlying, expiration, multiplier, and deliverable**, one contract each. **Fees, interest, dividends, taxes, and trading costs are $0 for classroom arithmetic.** Actual results must include them. Expiration bounds assume the matching position stays intact and exercise/settlement is handled consistently; they do not cover unwanted post-expiration stock, broken legs, or forced liquidation.

Your goal: identify what is owned, what is owed, cash paid/received, and a bad outcome for each position.

lessons.title: A long call buys upside exposure with a deadline
lessons.body:
A **long call** is a purchased right to buy shares at a strike. Used alone, it can benefit from a sufficiently large, timely rise. It can lose the full premium; it does not become good value simply because the premium is small. The option position's loss is limited to premium and costs, but exercising into stock creates a separate stock position and funding requirement. [OIC describes the long call](https://www.optionseducation.org/strategies/all-strategies/long-call).

**Worked example:** Buy one $50 call for $2. Pay **$200**. At expiration, stock at $56 gives `$6 × 100 = $600` exercise value and **$400 profit** after premium. Stock at $51 gives only $100 value and **$100 loss**, even though stock is above strike. At or below $50, the option loses its **$200 premium**. Expiration break-even is **$52**, before costs. Upside has no fixed theoretical ceiling as stock rises.

**Try it:** One $60 call costs $3. At expiration stock is $62. Find result, expiration break-even, and maximum option-premium loss.

<details><summary>Check your reasoning</summary>

Exercise value `(62 − 60) × 100 = $200`; subtract $300 premium: **−$100**. Break-even **$63**. Maximum premium loss **$300**, before costs and separate stock risks after exercise.

</details>

**Recall:** What three things can be wrong even if the buyer correctly expects an upward stock direction?

lessons.title: A long put buys downside exposure with a deadline
lessons.body:
A **long put** is a purchased right to sell at the strike. Used alone, it can benefit from a sufficiently large, timely stock fall. Its value can still fall before expiration if the stock move disappoints, IV drops, or time passes. [OIC describes the long put](https://www.optionseducation.org/strategies/all-strategies/long-put).

**Worked example:** Buy one $50 put for $2: pay **$200**. At expiration with stock $44, exercise value is `$6 × 100 = $600`; profit is **$400** after premium. With stock $49, exercise value is $100 and the result is **−$100**. At or above $50, the premium loss is **$200**. Expiration break-even is **$48**. Since a stock cannot fall below zero, idealized maximum expiration profit is `(50 − 2) × 100 = $4,800`, achieved at zero stock value before costs.

Exercising without owned shares can create short stock if allowed; the limited premium-loss statement applies to the option, not a later stock short.

**Try it:** One $40 put costs $1.50. Stock ends at $37. Find result and expiration break-even.

<details><summary>Check your reasoning</summary>

`[(40 − 37) − 1.50] × 100 = +$150`. Break-even **$38.50**. The calculation assumes a consistent expiration payoff; it is not a promise of a market sale or exercise workflow.

</details>

**Recall:** Why does a put have a finite theoretical expiration profit even if the stock collapses?

lessons.title: A protective put combines shares with a temporary floor
lessons.body:
A **protective put** combines owned stock and a matching long put. Buying both together is also called a **married put**. The put provides a sale right at the strike while it remains valid. Protection costs premium, has a deadline, and does not remove stock risk after it expires. [OIC explains a protective put](https://www.optionseducation.org/strategies/all-strategies/protective-put-married-put).

**Worked example:** Buy **100 shares at $50** and one **$45 put at $1**. Total initial cash outlay is `$5,000 + $100 = $5,100`. At expiration, if stock is $35, the shares are worth $3,500 and the put has $1,000 exercise value. Combined value is **$4,500**, a **$600 loss**. This is the idealized maximum expiration loss for this matched example: `(50 − 45 + 1) × 100`. At stock $60, the put has zero expiration value and the position is worth $6,000, a **$900 gain**.

The floor is $45/share in combined expiration value, not a promise that the original $50 purchase is protected completely. You paid another $1/share for that floor.

**Try it:** Buy 100 shares at $30 plus one $28 put for $0.80. What is total cost and the idealized maximum expiration loss?

<details><summary>Check your reasoning</summary>

Cost **$3,080**. Minimum combined expiration value is **$2,800** while the matched put protection applies. Maximum modeled expiration loss is **$280**, before excluded costs. Later protection requires a new decision and may cost more premium.

</details>

**Recall:** When does this protection stop applying?

lessons.title: A covered call exchanges some upside for premium
lessons.body:
A **covered call** combines 100 owned shares with one short call covering them. The shares cover delivery if assigned. They do not protect you against the stock collapsing. The short call can be assigned early, including around dividends, and limits the benefit from large stock rises. [OIC describes covered-call risk and foregone upside](https://www.optionseducation.org/strategies/all-strategies/covered-call-buy-write).

**Worked example:** Buy **100 shares at $50** and sell one **$55 call for $1**. Net outlay is **$4,900**. If stock ends at $60 and the call is exercised, sell the shares for $5,500. Profit is **$600**, and further stock upside does not increase that idealized expiration profit. At stock $40, the call has zero expiration value but shares are worth $4,000: **$900 loss**. At zero stock value, the loss is **$4,900**. The $100 premium was only a small cushion.

Do not describe this as risk-free income. Evaluate the whole stock-and-option position and whether giving up the shares at the strike serves the objective.

**Try it:** Buy 100 shares at $40 and sell one $45 call for $2. What is the idealized maximum expiration profit? What is the loss if stock becomes worthless?

<details><summary>Check your reasoning</summary>

Net outlay **$3,800**. Maximum expiration proceeds **$4,500**, so profit **$700**. At zero stock value, loss **$3,800** before costs. The short call's coverage fixes the share-delivery issue, not the stock's downside.

</details>

**Recall:** What does the word “covered” actually cover?

lessons.title: A cash-secured put reserves the money to buy shares
lessons.body:
A **cash-secured put** is a short put with enough cash set aside to fund its share purchase if assigned. It can result in buying stock after a sharp fall. Receiving premium does not eliminate the purchase obligation or the subsequent stock risk. [OIC describes the cash-secured put](https://www.optionseducation.org/strategies/all-strategies/cash-secured-put).

**Worked example:** Sell one **$45 put for $1** and reserve the **$4,500 exercise purchase amount**. Receive **$100 premium**. If assigned, pay $4,500 and receive 100 shares. The premium gives an economic acquisition cost of **$44/share before costs**. At stock $30, shares are worth $3,000, so the result including premium is **−$1,400**. At zero, maximum idealized loss is **$4,400**. Maximum option profit is the **$100 credit**, if no liability remains. Expiration break-even is $44.

Do not treat reserved cash as permission to buy stock you otherwise do not want or could not afford to lose. Broker collateral treatment must be checked separately.

**Try it:** Sell one $30 put for $0.80. State the exercise purchase amount, maximum idealized profit, break-even, and loss at zero stock value.

<details><summary>Check your reasoning</summary>

Purchase amount **$3,000**; maximum profit **$80**; break-even **$29.20**; loss at zero **$2,920**. All exclude costs. Assignment may occur before expiry, and cash must be available then.

</details>

**Recall:** Does receiving an $80 credit cap the writer's loss at $80?

lessons.title: A bull call debit spread trades away some upside to reduce cost
lessons.body:
A **bull call debit spread** buys one lower-strike call and sells one higher-strike call with matching terms. **Debit** means net cash paid. The short call reduces cost but caps the intact position's idealized expiration value. It also introduces assignment obligations. [OIC explains this spread](https://www.optionseducation.org/strategies/all-strategies/bull-call-spread-debit-call-spread).

**Worked example:** Buy one **$50 call for $3**; sell one **$55 call for $1**. Pay net `(3 − 1) × 100 = $200`. Strike width is $5, so the intact expiration value ranges from **$0 to $500**. Maximum modeled expiration loss is **$200**; maximum profit is **$300**; break-even is **$52**. At stock $53, the long call has $300 intrinsic value and the short call has zero, yielding **$100 profit** after the $200 debit.

If the short call is assigned early, the long call does not automatically exercise. Shares, funding, and order handling must be reconciled. The $200 bound is a matching-payoff statement, not a guarantee against every broken-leg or post-expiry outcome. [FINRA explains one-leg assignment](https://www.finra.org/investors/insights/trading-options-understanding-assignment).

**Try it:** A matching $40/$45 bull call spread costs $1.50 net. Find maximum modeled expiration loss, maximum profit, and break-even.

<details><summary>Check your reasoning</summary>

Loss **$150**; profit `(5 − 1.50) × 100 = $350`; break-even **$41.50**. Each result excludes costs and assumes the matching spread stays intact with exercise/settlement handled consistently.

</details>

**Recall:** What benefit of the long call did selling the higher call give up?

lessons.title: A bull put credit spread receives cash and keeps an obligation
lessons.body:
A **bull put credit spread** sells a higher-strike put and buys a lower-strike put with matching terms. **Credit** means net cash received. Profit is limited; losses arise when the stock falls far enough. The purchased put limits the intact expiration payoff loss under matching terms, not all operational funding needs. [OIC explains the bull put spread](https://www.optionseducation.org/strategies/all-strategies/bull-put-spread-credit-put-spread).

**Worked example:** Sell one **$50 put for $2** and buy one **$45 put for $1**. Net credit **$100**. At stock $55, both have zero expiration value: profit **$100**. At stock $48, the short put owes $200 exercise value while the long put has none: net result **−$100** after the initial credit. At or below $45, the intact payoff gap is $500: maximum modeled expiration loss **$400**. Break-even is **$49**.

Assignment of the short put can still require **$5,000 to buy 100 shares**, while the long put stays open. The long put's presence does not automatically submit the required exercise or closing instruction. [FINRA describes that operational risk](https://www.finra.org/investors/insights/trading-options-understanding-assignment).

**Try it:** A matching $35/$30 bull put spread receives $0.70 net. Calculate maximum profit, maximum modeled expiration loss, and break-even.

<details><summary>Check your reasoning</summary>

Profit **$70**; loss `(5 − 0.70) × 100 = $430`; break-even **$34.30**. Excludes costs and assumes consistent handling of the intact matching position. The credit is not the risk amount.

</details>

**Recall:** Why can a $430 modeled payoff loss coexist with a much larger temporary share-purchase amount?

lessons.title: Complexity is optional; “no trade” is a complete decision
lessons.body:
Names such as **straddle**, **strangle**, **calendar**, **butterfly**, and **iron condor** describe combinations of options. A straddle, for example, buys or sells a call and a put at the same strike and expiration. More legs create more terms, execution costs, and possible paths to understand. Different expirations leave live options at different times. You can study these later in [the reference volumes](LESSONS_01_FOUNDATIONS.md); you do not need to trade them to complete the beginner course.

**Worked example:** One call costs $2 and one put costs $2 at the same $50 strike and expiration. Buying both costs **$400**. At expiration with stock still $50, both have zero value and the full **$400 is lost** before costs. Owning a position for each direction did not make a profit inevitable. Large moves might help, but their price and timing matter. [OIC describes a long straddle](https://www.optionseducation.org/strategies/all-strategies/long-straddle).

When the contract is unclear, a single contract is too large, or an event exceeds what you can assess, a complete learning ticket can say **“no trade; continue observation.”** You do not need to choose a strategy merely because you studied it.

**Try it:** A hypothetical position risks $180, but your prewritten practice limit is $100. Does adding a strategy name or rounding up the limit solve the problem? State the decision.

<details><summary>Check your reasoning</summary>

No. One position exceeds the limit. Record **no trade** and the reason, or continue simulation. A more complicated position is a new analysis, not automatic permission to exceed an existing rule.

</details>

**Recall:** What useful evidence does a documented no-trade decision provide?

1. Call expires with zero intrinsic: **−$200**. Put has $300 exercise value minus $200 premium: **+$100**. Each option's maximum premium loss is **$200** before costs and separate stock exposure after exercise.
2. Cost **$4,100**. Floor while the matched protection applies is $3,800 combined expiration value, giving maximum modeled expiration loss **$300**. The put expires; later stock risk is not covered by that expired right.
3. Net covered-call outlay **$3,850**; capped proceeds $4,500; maximum profit **$650**. Loss at zero **$3,850**. The cash-secured put receives $100 premium but assignment requires **$3,500 to buy 100 shares**. It may suffer substantial losses if stock falls.
4. Call spread: loss **$200**, profit **$300**, break-even **$52**. Put spread: profit **$100**, loss **$400**, break-even **$49**. These are intact matching-expiration results before costs; funding and broken-leg outcomes require a separate ledger.
